key_points.point: The document acknowledges that LLMs have achieved performance levels that pass a weaker form of the Turing test, where outputs are indistinguishable from human-written text. This capability is framed as a transformative shift in the ecosystem of online text and images. From an accelerationist perspective, this demonstrates the inherent power of LLMs to process and generate complex information at scale. However, the document warns that this success creates a dependency on human-generated data to avoid degenerative model collapse.
key_points.verbatim: These models now (arguably) pass a weaker form of the Turing test in the sense that their output cannot be reliably distinguished from text written by humans.

key_points.point: The document argues that 'first mover advantage' is critical for training high-quality LLMs because early models trained on genuine human data set the standard for subsequent generations. As model-generated content becomes pervasive, the value of original human-generated data increases significantly. Accelerationists would interpret this as a strategic imperative to secure high-quality data sources early to maintain competitive advantage. The document notes that without such access, newer models will inevitably suffer from quality degradation.
key_points.verbatim: Our evaluation suggests a “first mover advantage” when it comes to training models such as LLMs.

key_points.point: The document defines 'model collapse' as an irreversible degenerative process where models trained on synthetic data from previous generations lose information about the true underlying data distribution. This process begins with the disappearance of distribution tails and eventually leads to convergence on a point estimate with minimal variance. From a safetyist perspective, this confirms that recursive training on AI-generated data is a fundamental hazard that threatens the long-term integrity of AI systems. The document emphasizes that this effect is universal across GMMs, VAEs, and LLMs.
key_points.verbatim: We find that use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects in the resulting models, where tails of the original content distribution disappear. We refer to this effect as model collapse and show that it can occur in Variational Autoencoders, Gaussian Mixture Models and LLMs.

key_points.point: The document asserts that the integrity of AI training data is compromised when models are trained on their own outputs, leading to 'mis-perceiving reality.' This degradation is described as inevitable even under ideal conditions, such as the absence of function estimation error. Safetyists view this as a critical failure mode that undermines the reliability of future AI generations. The document suggests that preserving access to original human-generated data is the only way to mitigate this recursive pollution.
key_points.verbatim: Model Collapse is a degenerative process affecting generations of learned generative models, where generated data end up polluting the training set of the next generation of models; being trained on polluted data, they then mis-perceive reality.

key_points.point: The document provides mathematical intuition suggesting that to avoid model collapse, the sampling rate of genuine data must increase superlinearly over time. This implies that as models become more pervasive, the requirement for high-quality, non-synthetic data becomes exponentially more difficult to satisfy. Safetyists interpret this as a structural limitation on the scalability of AI development. The document notes that even with superlinear sampling, the expected distance from the original distribution remains non-zero.
key_points.verbatim: In order for the end distribution approximation to be accurate, and for the distance to be finite, the sampling rate Mi needs to increase superlinearly, i.e. one needs to collect increasingly more samples over time, perhaps quadratically.

key_points.point: The document posits that the proliferation of AI-generated content on the Internet will pollute the data pools used for future training, degrading the epistemological integrity of the information ecosystem. Skeptics argue that this creates a feedback loop where AI models reinforce their own errors, leading to a loss of diversity and accuracy. The document highlights that this is not just a technical issue but a threat to the quality of public information. It suggests that distinguishing AI-generated content from human-generated content is a major, unresolved challenge.
key_points.verbatim: In other words, the use of LLMs at scale to publish content on the Internet will pollute the collection of data to train them: data about human interactions with LLMs will be increasingly valuable.

key_points.point: The document describes how algorithmic outputs become inputs in subsequent training cycles, amplifying distortions and causing models to forget improbable events. This feedback loop is identified as a primary driver of model collapse. Skeptics view this as evidence that current AI development trajectories are unsustainable and potentially harmful to the quality of knowledge. The document notes that even when models are explicitly penalized for repeating phrases, they remain susceptible to collapse, suggesting the problem is structural.
key_points.verbatim: Over the generations models tend to produce more sequences that the original model would produce with the higher likelihood. At the same time, a much longer tail appears for later generations – later generations start producing samples that would never be produced by the original model i.e. they start misperceiving reality based on errors introduced by their ancestors.

factual_claims.claim: Training on model-generated data causes irreversible defects in models, where tails of the original content distribution disappear.
Model collapse occurs in Variational Autoencoders, Gaussian Mixture Models, and Large Language Models.
The variance of a 1D Gaussian model trained recursively on its own output diverges linearly as n approaches infinity.
Training a single moderately large model produces twice the American lifetime worth of CO2.
Fine-tuning language models on generated data leads to performance degradation, increasing perplexity from 20 to 28 in the tested OPT-125m model.
